title: Track 7, Lesson 7: Investing internationally - don't bet on one market alone
subtitle: Vietnam's market is only a very small part of the global economic picture.
whyItMatters: Investing only at home means betting your entire wealth on the fortunes of a single economy. Understanding geographic diversification helps you reduce single-country concentration risk, even though cost and complexity rise.
openingQuestion: Why should a Vietnamese investor consider putting part of their money into international markets?
openingOptions: Because international markets always grow distinctly faster than the domestic Vietnamese stock market does
Because under current law every Vietnamese investor is required to invest into international markets
Because investing in international markets carries absolutely no currency risk that needs worrying about
Because it reduces concentration risk in a single economy
explanation: Geographic diversification addresses a risk that sector diversification never touches: your entire wealth depending on one economy, one currency and one policy regime. The point to weigh is that it introduces a new risk in the exchange rate, and that correlations between markets rise during a crisis - exactly when you need them low. Even so, your income and your home are already entirely inside the country.

realWorldExample.description: Many retail investors in emerging markets place part of their portfolio (20-30%, say) into ETFs tracking the US or global markets, so as not to depend entirely on the swings of a single economy.

quiz.question: Which risk is specific to international investing and absent at home?
options: Interest rate risk, which does not exist domestically
Inflation risk, which only affects foreign assets
Liquidity risk, since international markets are smaller
Currency risk when converting returns back into VND
quiz.explanation: When you invest in assets priced in a foreign currency, the real return (converted into VND) depends on the asset's performance AND the exchange rate. A currency falling against the dong can cut the return even when the asset itself performed well.

quiz.question: You invest 10,000 USD in a US ETF and it rises 10% over the year. But over that year the dollar falls 5% against the dong. Roughly what is your real return in VND?
options: Exactly 10% - the exchange rate has no effect
About 15% (10% plus a further 5%)
About 5% (10% with 5% simply taken off)
quiz.explanation: Converted return = (1 + asset return) × (1 + currency move) − 1 = 1.10 × 0.95 − 1 ≈ 0.045 = 4.5%. A concrete example of how currency moves can eat a substantial part of an international investment's headline return.

quiz.question: Which kind of concentration risk does international investing reduce?
options: The risk of global rates rising together across every major market
The risk of everything resting on one economy, currency and legal system
The risk of an individual company in the portfolio going bankrupt
The risk of global inflation eroding every currency's purchasing power at once
quiz.explanation: A Vietnamese person lives on dong, works in Vietnam and owns a home in Vietnam - and if the portfolio is also entirely Vietnamese shares, everything depends on one economy. Geographic diversification unpicks some of that overlap.

quiz.question: What new risk appears when investing abroad?
options: Legal risk, since Vietnamese retail investors are banned from owning foreign assets
Liquidity risk, since foreign markets trade less actively than the domestic one
Currency risk - the return in dong depends on how that currency moves
Information risk, since foreign companies publish no financial statements
quiz.explanation: A US portfolio up 10% while the dollar falls 12% against the dong still leaves you down. This is the extra layer of risk - in exchange for no longer depending on a single economy.

quiz.question: How do Vietnamese retail investors most commonly reach international markets?
options: Transferring money abroad freely to invest, with no procedure required
Opening an account directly on the New York Stock Exchange with no intermediary at all
Buying foreign shares directly through a domestic brokerage account
Through a domestic fund or fund certificate that invests abroad on their behalf
quiz.explanation: Foreign exchange rules limit how much capital an individual can move abroad, so the common route is a domestic fund with a mandate to invest overseas. Checking that a channel is legal before transferring money is a step not to skip.

quiz.question: What international weighting is reasonable for a Vietnamese retail investor?
options: There is no single right figure; weigh cost, tax and how well you understand it
Exactly fifty percent of the portfolio, to balance the two markets equally
The whole portfolio should sit in developed markets, where risk is lower
None of it should go abroad, since currency risk always outweighs the benefit
quiz.explanation: Access costs, tax and whether you actually understand the market are all real constraints. A small but genuine allocation beats an ideal weighting on paper that you cannot sustain.

keyTakeaways: International investing reduces concentration risk in a single economy and currency
Currency risk is the distinctive factor: the real return combines the asset's performance with the currency move
The whole portfolio does not need to go abroad - a moderate weighting (20-30%, say) already cuts concentration risk substantially

practicePrompt.question: You invest 5,000 USD in a European ETF and it rises 12% over the year. But over that year the euro strengthens 3% against the dong. What happens to your real return in VND?
options: Higher than 12%, at about 15.4% (1.12 × 1.03 − 1), thanks to the euro strengthening against the dong
Exactly 12%, because the ETF's return has nothing whatsoever to do with movements in the euro-dong exchange rate
Lower than 12%, because a euro strengthening against the dong always reduces the converted return correspondingly
Impossible to calculate without knowing exactly what the original principal was in dong before converting to dollars
practicePrompt.explanation: The converted return combines the asset's performance with the currency move - here both work in your favour, compounding to more than the asset's own 12%.

summary.keyIdea: International investing reduces concentration risk in a single economy and currency
summary.commonMistake: Reading the idea as a phrase to remember rather than a principle to apply to real decisions.
summary.action: Currency risk is the distinctive factor: the real return combines the asset's performance with the currency move

application.title: Check it now
application.message: Look at your current portfolio and work out what percentage sits entirely in the Vietnamese market - if it is near 100%, consider setting a small part aside for international assets.
application.secondary: There is no need to overturn everything at once; even a moderate weighting cuts concentration risk.

sections.text: Vietnam's stock market is a very small piece of the global economic picture. If 100% of your invested assets are domestic, every economic or policy shock at home hits all of them at once, with nothing to offset it.

International investing reduces concentration risk in a single economy, a single currency and a single policy regime. Many retail investors in emerging markets place part of their portfolio, 20-30% say, into ETFs tracking the US or global markets - not to maximise returns, but to avoid depending entirely on the swings of one economy.
Currency risk - the factor unique to investing abroad

When you invest in assets priced in a foreign currency, the real return in dong depends on the asset's performance AND the currency move - two entirely independent factors. **Example:** you invest 10,000 USD in a US ETF and it rises 10% over the year. But over that year the dollar falls 5% against the dong. The converted return = (1 + 10%) × (1 − 5%) − 1 = 1.10 × 0.95 − 1 ≈ 4.5% - far below the 10% on the fund's own report, because the dollar's fall ate a substantial part of the headline gain.
The whole portfolio does not need to go abroad

The aim of international investing is not to move everything overseas, but to reduce how much depends on one market. A moderate weighting, 20-30% of the portfolio say, already cuts concentration risk substantially while leaving most of your assets where you understand them best and where you will be spending in dong in future.

items: Consider an international index ETF (tracking the S&P 500, MSCI World and so on) as the simplest starting point
Understand that the converted return combines the asset's performance with the currency move, rather than adding them
Start with a small weighting (10-20%) and raise it once you are used to the currency swings
You don't need to understand individual foreign companies - an international index fund is already diversified inside itself
